title: The Silence Clause in Médecins Sans Frontières' First Charter
dek: In December 1971 the doctors and journalists who founded MSF wrote into its charter a promise not to judge in public the forces they worked among.

story.founder: Raymond Borel, Philippe Bernier, Max Récamier, Bernard Kouchner and other founding doctors
story.event: Founding MSF with a charter that bound members to discretion
story.summary: Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in December 1971 when a group of French doctors back from the Biafra war merged with a volunteer pool set up by journalists at the medical paper Tonus. The charter drafted by Tonus editor Philippe Bernier bound members to strict neutrality and to refrain from publicly judging the forces and leaders who accepted their help; MSF replaced it in 1991 with a charter and a policy on bearing witness.
paragraphs: On 20 December 1971, by the account the medical paper Tonus printed that month, fifteen doctors met to lay the foundations of a new association, draft its charter, adopt statutes and elect a board. On 22 December Médecins Sans Frontières was voted into being. It joined two groups. One was doctors, among them Max Récamier and Bernard Kouchner, who had worked with the French Red Cross in Nigeria's civil war and on their return set up an emergency medical group. The other came from Tonus itself: the journalists Raymond Borel and Philippe Bernier, appalled at how little help reached East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, after the floods of 1970, had gathered a pool of volunteer doctors.

The Biafra doctors had seen civilians starved by blockade. MSF's own history says Récamier and Kouchner openly criticised the Nigerian government and the Red Cross, though one historian has found that the Red Cross reprinted their first newspaper article. Kouchner later said of the new group, "In the back of our minds was the fact that we'd already done this and we wanted to do it again."

Yet the charter Bernier drafted asked for discretion. Members were to work in strict neutrality, keep out of states' internal affairs and, under its fourth article, refrain from judging or publicly expressing any opinion, favourable or hostile, about the events, forces or leaders that had accepted their help. The statutes went further: no member could speak or write about the association or its missions without the board's special authorisation, on pain of immediate expulsion. Rony Brauman, MSF's president from 1982 to 1994, wrote that he had found no record of the founders' debates. His guess was that the young association wanted to reassure the governments of the countries where it hoped to work. Only a short majority of the founders, he noted, had been in Biafra.

The next day four founding members left for East Pakistan with the Red Cross; with little money, early volunteers went out through other agencies. The silence was argued over for years. In 1991 MSF adopted a new charter, dropping the ban on public judgment, and a policy on bearing witness. The story of an organisation born to speak out, Brauman wrote, took hold only in the late 1970s.

quote.text: Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity of his nature.  A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi ties restraint in speech to following one's own nature, and warns that sudden gusts do not last. MSF's founders put restraint on paper while some of them were known for protest, and twenty years later the organisation decided speech belonged to its nature. Which nature the first charter expressed stays open.

reflection: A founding document records what its authors feared and hoped at one moment. MSF's first charter promised discretion, perhaps to win trust from governments; twenty years later the organisation rewrote it to match what it had become, and the earlier version was not a lie for that.

You may carry rules of your own that were set early: to stay quiet in meetings until you had earned a place, or never to bring work worries home. Some of them still protect you. Others were written for a version of you that has since changed, and can be rewritten without shame.
invitation: Pick one rule you set yourself early on about when to speak up and when to stay quiet. Write it as you would phrase it today, then keep whichever version is truer.

sources.supports: Founding by doctors and journalists on 22 December 1971; the Biafra doctors' emergency group (GIMCU) and the Tonus journalists' Secours Médical Français, formed after the 1970 Bangladesh floods; Bernier drafting the charter; Tonus No. 493 (December 1971): fifteen doctors meeting on 20 December to draft the charter, adopt statutes and elect a board, and four founding members leaving for eastern Pakistan with the Red Cross on 23 December; the 1971 statutes signed by ten doctors including Récamier and Kouchner plus Bernier and Borel; statutes article 8 prohibiting public statements without the board's authorisation on pain of immediate expulsion; early volunteers sent abroad through other organisations for lack of money.

cross_checks.claim: MSF was founded in December 1971 by doctors who had worked in Biafra together with journalists from the medical paper Tonus, Raymond Borel and Philippe Bernier.
The 1971 charter bound members to neutrality, non-interference in states' internal affairs and abstaining from publicly judging the events, forces or leaders who accepted their help.
MSF adopted a new charter in 1991 that dropped the ban on public judgment, alongside a policy on bearing witness.
Max Récamier and Bernard Kouchner had worked with the Red Cross in Biafra during Nigeria's civil war before founding MSF.

research_notes: The slate framed this as 'founding a medical group that would speak out' and credited Bernard Kouchner first. The documents say otherwise. MSF's own archive copy of the December 1971 charter, drafted by Tonus editor Philippe Bernier, bound members to neutrality and to abstain from publicly judging the forces they worked among, and the 1971 statutes (article 8, quoted in MSF's associative history) banned unauthorised public statements on pain of expulsion. Rony Brauman, MSF president 1982-1994, calls the speaking-out origin story a myth that took hold at the end of the 1970s, citing Marie-Luce Desgrandchamps (Relations internationales no. 146, 2011, not checked directly because cairn.info blocks automated requests). MSF Ireland's history page still says Récamier and Kouchner openly criticised the Nigerian government and the Red Cross; the story attributes that to MSF and notes the historian's contrary finding. The story therefore tells the founding as a decision for discretion and names several founders. Founders: the 1971 statutes list ten doctors (Bérès, Cabrol, Delcourt, Grellety Bosviel, Illiouz, Kouchner, Pigeon, Radoman, Récamier, Wild) plus Bernier and Borel; MSF South Asia lists thirteen, adding Xavier Emmanuelli; Tonus said fifteen doctors met on 20 December. The story uses Tonus's fifteen for that meeting and gives no total for founders. Dates: Tonus says the founders met on 20 December and the vote was on 22 December; Raymond Borel later wrote 'born on 20 December 1971'; MSF's chronology gives 22 December as the creation date; the story gives both. Both dates come from MSF's own archive (no independent loadable page states the day), so they are not listed as a cross-check. The 1970 disaster is called 'the 1970 Bangladesh floods' in MSF's history (the Bhola cyclone, in what was then East Pakistan); the story follows MSF's wording. Brauman's English article (IRRC No. 888) loads only as an abstract at cambridge.org and is blocked at international-review.icrc.org, so the French edition on icrc.org is cited; it is a compressed PDF and does not register names for the automated checker, though it loads. MSF's associative history is a 400-page PDF; the founding section (pages 23-25) and the 1979 general assembly were read in full. Kouchner's quotation is from MSF Ireland's page and is undated. The Laozi passage is about following the Tao, applied here by analogy.
